judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 4 Indicators (same rank 0) in Strand 3 Geometry and Measurement, Sub-strand 3 Measurement- (Perimeter and Area), but under different Content Standards: B4.3.3.1 (perimeter of regular/irregular shapes) and B4.3.3.2 (area of regular/irregular 2-D shapes). 'Measure and record perimeter for regular and irregular shapes in cm and m' and 'Recognise that area is measured in square units' are complementary measurement-attribute skills that reinforce each other by contrasting linear units (cm, m) with square units for area within the same measurement sub-strand. The available evidence (shared sub-strand, LC texts, and code-prefix/local-rank proximity, which are weak signals only) shows substantive conceptual coherence but does not substantiate a same-rank developmental dependency in either direction: proficiency in recording perimeter in cm/m is not shown to be required or to materially support recognising square units as the area unit, nor the reverse. Source-code ordering (B4.3.3.1.2 before B4.3.3.2.1) is not treated as positive developmental evidence.

judgment.rationale: Both endpoints are BASIC 5 Indicators (same grain, same rank 1), so direction rests on statement content rather than coordinate gap. B5.1.2.1.2 asks learners to apply mental multiplication strategies (annexing then adding zeros, halving and doubling, use of the distributive property) under a content standard on mental mathematics strategies and basic multiplication facts to 81. B5.1.2.2.1 asks learners to multiply multi-digit numbers by 2-digit numbers efficiently, under a content standard on multiplication of 2- or 3-digit numbers by 2- or 3-digit numbers. The named strategies (annexing zeros, distributive decomposition) are precisely the reasoning tools that make multi-digit by 2-digit multiplication 'efficient', so fluency with the mental strategies indicator supports success on the multi-digit efficiency indicator; the reverse dependency is not supported. Hierarchy evidence is weak because both items carry unresolved ancestry with framework-root fallback, and source evidence is truncated for both, so this judgment rests on the trustworthy statement text and grade coordinate only; hence moderate confidence.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 6 (rank 2) Indicators in Strand 4: Data, Sub-strand 1 (Data Collection, Organization, Presentation, Interpretation and Analysis), so they share the same statement-type grain and the same coordinate rank. First (B6.4.1.1.2, under Content Standard B6.4.1.1 on creating/labelling/interpreting line graphs) asks pupils to judge whether a data set is continuous (line graph) or discrete (series of points) and justify the choice; second (under Content Standard B6.4.1.2 on selecting and using data-collection methods) asks pupils to design and administer a questionnaire and record the results. These are complementary phases of the same data-handling cycle (collecting/recording data vs. deciding on an appropriate representation), and the LC sets are distinct (questionnaire design/administration/recording vs. continuous/discrete representation reasoning) with only the generic token 'data' shared. At equal rank there is no substantive evidence that proficiency in either specifically supports success in the other — questionnaire data is not necessarily the data judged for line-graph suitability — so symmetric relatesTo, not buildsTowards. Evidence limits: both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each), and the second endpoint has a code anomaly (statement_code null, source excerpt shows 'B6.5.2.2' while its resolved parent is B6.4.1.2 and context labels reference B6.4.1.1); this code inconsistency was not used as positive hierarchy evidence.

These are complementary phases of the same data-handling cycle (collecting/recording data vs. deciding on an appropriate representation), and the LC sets are distinct (questionnaire design/administration/recording vs. continuous/discrete representation reasoning) with only the generic token 'data' shared. At equal rank there is no substantive evidence that proficiency in either specifically supports success in the other — questionnaire data is not necessarily the data judged for line-graph suitability — so symmetric relatesTo, not buildsTowards. Evidence limits: both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each), and the second endpoint has a code anomaly (statement_code null, source excerpt shows 'B6.5.2.2' while its resolved parent is B6.4.1.2 and context labels reference B6.4.1.1); this code inconsistency was not used as positive hierarchy evidence.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 4 Indicators (same grain, same rank 0) under the same percent Content Standard text (B4.1.5.1). B4.1.5.1.1 establishes the foundational concept of percent as a fraction related to hundredths through concrete models, pictures and the number line; B4.1.5.1.2 then requires comparing and ordering a mixture of common, decimal and percent fractions up to hundredths. Recognising and modelling percent as hundredths is the conceptual basis that makes cross-representation comparison and ordering achievable, so proficiency in the second supports success in the first — a substantive same-rank developmental step, not mere wording or code-prefix overlap. Hierarchy evidence is discounted because both endpoints carry unresolved-ancestry framework-root fallback; the judgment rests on statement text and source excerpts, which are consistent though partially truncated.

judgment.rationale: Both endpoints are BASIC 4 Indicators (rank 0, same grade coordinate) in Strand 1 NUMBER, Sub-strand 3: Fractions, so any developmental direction would need substantive same-rank evidence. B4.1.3.2.1 concerns comparing and ordering like-denominator fractions via pictorial representations and equivalent fractions with the LCD (LCs: compare/order fractions, LCD, pictorial), while B4.1.3.1.4 concerns recognising, drawing and labelling improper fractions (LCs: recognise/draw/label improper fractions). These are complementary Basic 4 fraction-representation skills that reinforce one another (pictorial modelling and symbolic labelling of fractions), but neither statement's proficiency is shown by the bounded evidence to be a substantive enabler of the other: improper-fraction recognition is not required to compare like-denominator fractions, and comparing/ordering does not extend into improper-fraction notation. Source code prefix, page proximity and the single shared token 'fractions' are weak nomination signals only, and the parent Content Standards carry a known Basic 4 Fractions editorial code anomaly (B4.1.3.1/B4.1.3.2 merge context), which further weakens any code-order-based directional inference. Symmetric conceptual coherence is supported; dependency is not.
